We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

New tasks at each station: What published work has one arm take over several hands-on laboratory tasks at different instruments (swapping vial carriers on a pipetting gantry, augers or hoppers on a powder doser, tool changers, capping, weighing, loading plates), what positioning tolerance did each task need, and what success rates were reported? How were new tasks added (teach pendant or scripted waypoints, fiducial-guided motion, or imitation-learning policies such as ACT, diffusion policy or LeRobot policies), how many demonstrations or how much setup time did each need, and how do they compare on the same task?

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

# Tests and Benchmarks for Robot Arms as Automated Manual Manipulators in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Robot Arms Performing Multiple Hands-On Tasks at Different Stations

The most comprehensive demonstration of a single arm taking over several hands-on laboratory tasks at different instruments is the mobile robotic chemist by Burger et al. (2020), which used a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on a KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR) platform. Over eight days it autonomously performed 688 experiments across multiple stations encompassing weighing and dispensing insoluble solids, dispensing liquid solutions, transporting sample vials in racks, capping vials under nitrogen, sonication for catalyst dispersion, photolysis, and transferring samples to a head-space gas chromatograph (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). In robustness tests the system achieved 464/464 successful vial grasps and placements and 400/400 successful cartridge grasps and placements at both the hotel and the Quantos dispenser, over 29 and 25 iterations respectively (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 69-73). The cartridge cavity was only 0.5 mm larger than the cartridge, implying a placement tolerance of approximately 0.25 mm (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 69-73). The arm had a stated repeatability of 0.1 mm, and after six-point touch-sensitive calibration against a reference cube, the station frame was located to within 0.12 mm with orientation residuals below 0.005° (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56).

Jiang et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1039/D3DD00075C) demonstrated an ABB YuMi dual-arm robot performing biomimetic solid dispensing. Tasks included opening and closing an analytical-balance door, moving vials and hoppers, selecting and manipulating spatulas of different sizes, scooping powder, dispensing through a funnel, and closed-loop weighing (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 3-4). The system dispensed thirteen different solids at target weights down to 20 ± 2 mg. For non-challenging solids at 200 mg, the mean dispensing error was 0.07%; across all solids the mean failure rate was 23.1% over 120 runs, where failure was defined as non-completion of one dispensing procedure (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11). Failure causes included blocked funnels, deliquescent material, and robot errors when the balance showed no weight change during continuous dispensing (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10).

Lunt et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1039/D3SC06206F) presented a multi-robot integration for a 12-step PXRD workflow using an ABB YuMi and KUKA KMR. The YuMi transferred vials from transport racks to a grinding station, carried out grinding-related handling, unscrewed vial caps, and placed caps into a plate at the sample-preparation station (lunt2024aroboticworkflow pages 87-95). The KMR provided mobile base precision of ±10 mm and orientation below ±2.5°, with fine calibration achieved via force-feedback six-point calibration cubes (lunt2024aroboticworkflow pages 49-57). No task-level success rate was reported for this system.

ORGANA (Darvish et al., 2025; DOI: 10.1016/j.matt.2024.10.015) used a Franka robot to perform solubility screening (7 steps, 25.63 min), recrystallization (8 steps, 44.80 min), pH measurement (6 steps, 3.85 min), and electrochemistry including electrode polishing (114 steps, 130 min) (darvish2025organaarobotic pages 14-15). No positioning tolerance or success rate was reported.

OSCAR (Pivin et al., 2026; DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733) used a UR3 arm to perform pipetting (1–200 µL), tip handling, PCR thermocycler programming via a stylus tool, gel electrophoresis loading, Petri-dish manipulation, spreading, and colony picking across three multistep biology protocols. The same protocols were successfully replanned for UR5 and Franka Panda arms, with average planning time of approximately 5 s across all three arm models (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 7-8). No positioning tolerance or task-level success rate was reported.

Lim et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1109/TASE.2020.3036055) used a Denso VS-060 6-DOF arm to automate a Michael reaction, performing syringe-pump liquid transfer, mixing on a magnetic stirrer, silica/cotton filtration, and vial transfer to a GC-MS autoinjector rack. The robot achieved a yield of 34%, which was stated to be "comparable to that obtained by a junior chemist (undergraduate student in Chemistry)" (lim2021developmentofa pages 1-2). No positioning tolerance was reported; yields rather than manipulation success rates served as the outcome metric.

## 2. Positioning Tolerances by Task

The literature reveals a hierarchy of positioning demands:

- **Cartridge/hopper placement into powder dispensers**: ~0.25 mm, as the cavity clearance is only 0.5 mm larger than the cartridge (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 69-73).
- **Syringe injection into a GC port**: ≤1.50 mm needle-tip error, as the injection port radius is 1.50 mm (angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 2-3, angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 4-6).
- **Vial grasping and placement**: The KUKA system achieved 0.12 mm calibrated accuracy sufficient for 100% success on 10 mL GC vials (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56).
- **Solid dispensing (mass tolerance rather than position)**: ±2 mg at 20 mg targets; 0.07% mean error at 200 mg for non-challenging solids (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 2-3).
- **Mobile base coarse positioning**: ±10 mm and ±2.5° before fine arm calibration (lunt2024aroboticworkflow pages 49-57).

**Explicit gap**: No study reports the positioning tolerance required for swapping vial carriers on a pipetting gantry, loading well plates into plate readers, or changing augers/hoppers on a powder doser as a reproducible benchmark with a defined tolerance threshold. These tasks appear in descriptions of SDL workflows but without quantified manipulation requirements.

## 3. Station Recalibration Methods

Three distinct approaches to recalibration at each station have been published:

**Touch-sensitive calibration cubes (Burger et al., 2020)**: The KUKA LBR iiwa touches six points on three mutually perpendicular faces of a calibration cube at each station, and the recorded contact points define the station coordinate frame relative to the robot. With initial position noise of up to ±15 mm and orientation noise of ±2.5°, the cube was located to within 0.12 mm and orientation offsets were reduced below 0.005° (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). This is the closest published analog to an AprilTag-based calibration square, but uses force feedback rather than vision.

**AprilTag coarse localization plus visual servoing (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; DOI: 10.1109/IROS55552.2023.10341743)**: An AprilTag brought the end effector near the injection target, then two fixed cameras and a Keypoint-RCNN model detected the syringe needle and iteratively servoed to submillimeter alignment. This achieved 100% injection success over 63 trials, while the AprilTag-only approach achieved only 9.52% (2160p) and 4.76% (1080p) (angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 7-8, angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 4-6). This demonstrates that AprilTag-only localization is insufficient for millimeter-precision tasks and must be supplemented with closed-loop visual refinement.

**Semantic object models with precision fixtures (OSCAR, Pivin et al., 2026)**: Each piece of labware is characterized in a Semantic Object Description Format (SODF) encoding 3D shape, interaction points, and forces. Objects are anchored with precision shoulder screws and 3D-printed supports; the system then uses position and force control to interact with them (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 3-5). This is a teaching-agnostic approach where new layouts require re-fixturing rather than re-programming.

**ALVAR fiducial tags (Joshi, 2021)**: ALVAR tags attached to objects supported object detection and pose estimation in a dual-arm system using cameras, Kinect, and force/torque sensors (joshi2021optimizationandapplication pages 35-39). This is the most direct precedent for AprilTag-based fiducial-guided motion in a laboratory manipulator context.

**Explicit gap**: No publication describes a system that uses AprilTags (specifically) as calibration squares at each station in a materials-science SDL to recalibrate a low-cost arm before each task, as the user describes. The Angelopoulos approach is the closest, but uses AprilTags only for coarse approach, not as the primary calibration target.

*Table: Comparison of published approaches for adding robot-arm tasks, from deterministic waypoint programming and fiducial-guided servoing to LeRobot imitation learning and reinforcement learning. Reported demonstration budgets and success rates are kept distinct from qualitative demonstrations and chemical-yield outcomes.*

### 4.1 Teach Pendant and Scripted Waypoints

The dominant approach in published SDL work is deterministic programming via teach pendants or scripted waypoints. Burger et al. used station-specific programs with six-point tactile recalibration (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). Joshi (2021) described the ABB YuMi's RS-2 system where "job teaching" stores motion elements, labware-specific gripper indices, and reference points, explicitly rejecting path planning as "unsafe, difficult to reconfigure, computationally demanding" (joshi2021optimizationandapplication pages 66-69). OSCAR's approach generates robot behaviors from digital models of labware and a calibrated workspace map rather than from device-specific waypoint recording (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 3-5). This yields extremely high reliability where tested (464/464, 400/400), but the programming time per new task is not measured in any study.

### 4.2 Imitation Learning Policies on Low-Cost Arms

The most directly relevant study for the user's setup is Cowling (2026; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170; **preprint**), which evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0.5 on an SO-101 leader/follower arm (approximately $200 in parts) using LeRobot's implementations. The task was picking up a green ball while ignoring two red distractors and placing it in a basket, with success defined as delivery within 30 seconds. One operator recorded 225 demonstrations by leader-follower teleoperation at 30 fps; each demonstration lasted approximately 17 seconds. Nested training sets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations were evaluated on 10 fixed placements (cowling2026from12to pages 5-7, cowling2026from12to pages 7-9).

Key results (cowling2026from12to pages 9-12):
- **ACT from scratch**: 1/40 (2.5%) at 12 demos → 37/40 (92.5%) at 100 demos, with an odds ratio of 3.89 per doubling of data. This is the recommended LeRobot baseline for ≥100 demonstrations.
- **π0.5 expert-only fine-tuning**: 16/40 (40%) at 12 demos → 28/40 (70%) at 25 demos, then stable around 68–75%. This provides a large advantage with scarce data but saturates below ACT's peak.
- **Diffusion Policy (trimmed)**: Peaked at 25/50 (50%) with 50 demonstrations but was non-monotonic. Untrimmed data yielded only 3/110 successes; removing a median 2.8 s idle lead-in was essential.
- **SmolVLA**: Peaked at 21/40 (52.5%) at 50 demos and declined with more data.
- **π0.5 LoRA fine-tuning**: 4/110 total successes; this recipe largely failed.

The study's evaluation protocol is reproducible: each block comprised one checkpoint run once on each of 10 placements in order, with a 30-second limit per episode and a 20-second reset. All 1,340 main-comparison episodes were scored and audited against recordings (cowling2026from12to pages 7-9).

**Explicit gap**: No published work has applied ACT, Diffusion Policy, or any LeRobot-style imitation-learning policy to a laboratory instrument task (e.g., capping, pipetting, weighing, plate loading) on a low-cost arm. The Cowling study used a pick-and-place task with distractor objects, not a chemistry workflow. Extending these results to the constrained, precision-demanding tasks of an SDL requires new experiments.

### 4.3 Reinforcement Learning

Pizzuto et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1109/CASE59546.2024.10711291) demonstrated model-free RL (TQC with Hindsight Experience Replay) for vial scraping on a Franka Emika Panda. The policy used proprioceptive feedback and force/torque readings; no human demonstrations were required. The real-robot case study succeeded with two vial sizes and two scraper lengths, with each full-vial scrape taking approximately 90 minutes across 24 regions (pizzuto2024acceleratinglaboratoryautomation pages 6-7). Curriculum learning was essential for generalizing across starting poses (pizzuto2024acceleratinglaboratoryautomation pages 4-6). No repeated-trial success percentage was reported; the only non-recoverable failure was a stuck scraper requiring human reset (pizzuto2024acceleratinglaboratoryautomation pages 7-8).

Lei et al. (2026; DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.aed6267) achieved 1000/1000 successful episodes across eight manipulation tasks by combining diffusion-policy imitation learning with offline and online RL. Per task, approximately 115 demonstrations (1.8 hours of human teleoperation), 566 offline RL rollouts (6.5 hours), and 434 online RL rollouts (5.6 hours) were needed—approximately 13.9 hours total (lei2026performantroboticmanipulation pages 12-15). This was not demonstrated in an SDL context, but the protocol establishes a reproducible benchmark for deployment-grade manipulation learning.

## 5. Cost Considerations

**No published cost-per-task metric exists** for comparing robot arms in SDL applications. The literature provides only broad cost ranges:

- Commercial articulated robots (KUKA, ABB, UR, Franka) are described as generally costing approximately $20,000–$40,000 for the arm alone (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 24-24). Complete mobile platforms such as the KUKA KMR are substantially more expensive (generally considered over $100,000).
- Burger's thesis notes that combining a MiR mobile base with a UR5 or Franka Panda provides "a dexterous collaborative mobile robot similar to the KMR at a lower purchase price" but gives no figures (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 49-52).
- 3D-printed and open-source robotic arms range from $50 (DeltaZ) to $700 (anthropomorphic arm with vision-based manipulation) (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 24-25).
- The SO-101 arm used in the Cowling (2026) study costs "a few hundred dollars in parts" (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3).

**Explicit gap**: No study compares the cost per task—or cost per successfully completed laboratory operation—between industry-standard arms (UR5e at ~$35k, Franka Panda at ~$30k, ABB YuMi at ~$40k) and low-cost alternatives (AgileX PiPER at ~$2k, SO-101 at ~$200). Such a metric would need to account for arm cost, integration time, programming or training time per task, success rate, cycle time, and maintenance. This represents a significant gap that the user's work could fill.

## 6. Reproducible Test Protocols Identified

Based on the literature, the following tests can be reproduced by anyone validating an affordable arm for SDL use:

1. **Vial grasp-and-place (Burger protocol)**: Grasp 10 mL GC vials from a rack, navigate to a target station, and place into a receiving rack. Repeat for N iterations. Measure: success/failure (vial placed without dropping); number of trials ≥400; success criterion: vial seated in well; measuring tool: visual inspection or force-feedback contact confirmation (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 69-73).

2. **Cartridge/hopper insertion (Burger protocol)**: Place a cartridge into a cavity with 0.5 mm clearance. Measure: successful insertion (cartridge seated); number of trials ≥400; success criterion: cartridge detected in position; measuring tool: force-feedback confirmation (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 69-73).

3. **Syringe injection alignment (Angelopoulos protocol)**: Align a syringe needle with a 1.50 mm radius target. Measure: XY planar distance between needle tip and target center after alignment; number of trials ≥63; success criterion: needle tip within 1.50 mm of target center; measuring tool: two calibrated machine-vision cameras with Keypoint-RCNN detection (angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 4-6, angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 6-7).

4. **Solid dispensing accuracy (Jiang protocol)**: Dispense 13 different solids at multiple target weights (1000, 500, 200, 20 mg). Measure: percentage dispensing error = (dispensed − target)/target × 100; number of runs: 120 total; success criterion: completed procedure within mass tolerance; measuring tool: analytical balance; failure criterion: non-completion of one procedure (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 7-8).

5. **Imitation-learning data-efficiency scaling (Cowling protocol)**: Train ACT/Diffusion Policy/foundation models on nested demonstration sets of 12, 25, 50, 100, 200 episodes. Evaluate each checkpoint on 10 fixed placements with a 30-second time limit. Measure: successes/episodes with 95% Wilson score intervals; criterion: target object delivered to goal; measuring tool: operator scoring audited against camera recordings (cowling2026from12to pages 5-7, cowling2026from12to pages 7-9, cowling2026from12to pages 9-12).

6. **Six-point calibration accuracy (Burger protocol)**: Touch six points on three perpendicular faces of a calibration cube with known initial noise. Measure: residual position error (mm) and orientation error (degrees); measuring tool: force-feedback contact detection; success criterion: frame located within specification (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56).

## 7. Explicit Gaps in the Published Literature

The following specific gaps were identified where **no published evidence exists**:

1. **No study has used imitation learning (ACT, Diffusion Policy, or any LeRobot policy) for a laboratory instrument task** such as capping, pipetting, weighing, or plate loading on any arm, let alone a low-cost one.

2. **No cost-per-task metric** has been published comparing industry-standard and affordable arms for SDL operations.

3. **No study has used AprilTags as the primary calibration target** (calibration square) at each station for a robot arm in a materials-science SDL. The Angelopoulos AprilTag + visual-servoing approach and Burger's touch-calibration-cube approach are the closest analogs.

4. **No study has benchmarked an AgileX PiPER or SO-101 arm** on any laboratory instrument task. The SO-101 has been evaluated only on a pick-and-place task with distractor objects.

5. **No study reports positioning tolerance requirements for swapping vial carriers on a pipetting gantry**, loading/unloading augers or hoppers on a powder doser, or performing tool changes in a materials-science context as reproducible benchmarks.

6. **Task-level success rates are rarely reported** with sufficient statistical rigor: Burger (100%, ≥400 trials), Angelopoulos (100%, 63 trials), and Jiang (76.9%, 120 runs) are exceptions. Most SDL papers describe workflow demonstrations without systematic success/failure counting.

7. **Setup time and programming time per new task** are not measured in any SDL robotics paper. This information is essential for comparing the value proposition of teach-pendant programming against imitation learning but is entirely absent from the literature.

# Tests and Benchmarks for Robot Arms as Automated Manual Manipulators in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Robot Arms Performing Multiple Hands-On Tasks at Different Stations

The most comprehensive demonstration of a single arm taking over several hands-on laboratory tasks at different instruments is the mobile robotic chemist by Burger et al. (2020), which used a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on a KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR) platform. Over eight days it autonomously performed 688 experiments across multiple stations encompassing weighing and dispensing insoluble solids, dispensing liquid solutions, transporting sample vials in racks, capping vials under nitrogen, sonication for catalyst dispersion, photolysis, and transferring samples to a head-space gas chromatograph (pqac-00000037). In robustness tests the system achieved 464/464 successful vial grasps and placements and 400/400 successful cartridge grasps and placements at both the hotel and the Quantos dispenser, over 29 and 25 iterations respectively (pqac-00000011). The cartridge cavity was only 0.5 mm larger than the cartridge, implying a placement tolerance of approximately 0.25 mm (pqac-00000011). The arm had a stated repeatability of 0.1 mm, and after six-point touch-sensitive calibration against a reference cube, the station frame was located to within 0.12 mm with orientation residuals below 0.005° (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000038).

Jiang et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1039/D3DD00075C) demonstrated an ABB YuMi dual-arm robot performing biomimetic solid dispensing. Tasks included opening and closing an analytical-balance door, moving vials and hoppers, selecting and manipulating spatulas of different sizes, scooping powder, dispensing through a funnel, and closed-loop weighing (pqac-00000029). The system dispensed thirteen different solids at target weights down to 20 ± 2 mg. For non-challenging solids at 200 mg, the mean dispensing error was 0.07%; across all solids the mean failure rate was 23.1% over 120 runs, where failure was defined as non-completion of one dispensing procedure (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000032). Failure causes included blocked funnels, deliquescent material, and robot errors when the balance showed no weight change during continuous dispensing (pqac-00000030).

Lunt et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1039/D3SC06206F) presented a multi-robot integration for a 12-step PXRD workflow using an ABB YuMi and KUKA KMR. The YuMi transferred vials from transport racks to a grinding station, carried out grinding-related handling, unscrewed vial caps, and placed caps into a plate at the sample-preparation station (pqac-00000028). The KMR provided mobile base precision of ±10 mm and orientation below ±2.5°, with fine calibration achieved via force-feedback six-point calibration cubes (pqac-00000027). No task-level success rate was reported for this system.

ORGANA (Darvish et al., 2025; DOI: 10.1016/j.matt.2024.10.015) used a Franka robot to perform solubility screening (7 steps, 25.63 min), recrystallization (8 steps, 44.80 min), pH measurement (6 steps, 3.85 min), and electrochemistry including electrode polishing (114 steps, 130 min) (pqac-00000018). No positioning tolerance or success rate was reported.

OSCAR (Pivin et al., 2026; DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733) used a UR3 arm to perform pipetting (1–200 µL), tip handling, PCR thermocycler programming via a stylus tool, gel electrophoresis loading, Petri-dish manipulation, spreading, and colony picking across three multistep biology protocols. The same protocols were successfully replanned for UR5 and Franka Panda arms, with average planning time of approximately 5 s across all three arm models (pqac-00000055). No positioning tolerance or task-level success rate was reported.

Lim et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1109/TASE.2020.3036055) used a Denso VS-060 6-DOF arm to automate a Michael reaction, performing syringe-pump liquid transfer, mixing on a magnetic stirrer, silica/cotton filtration, and vial transfer to a GC-MS autoinjector rack. The robot achieved a yield of 34%, which was stated to be "comparable to that obtained by a junior chemist (undergraduate student in Chemistry)" (pqac-00000014). No positioning tolerance was reported; yields rather than manipulation success rates served as the outcome metric.

## 2. Positioning Tolerances by Task

The literature reveals a hierarchy of positioning demands:

- **Cartridge/hopper placement into powder dispensers**: ~0.25 mm, as the cavity clearance is only 0.5 mm larger than the cartridge (pqac-00000011).
- **Syringe injection into a GC port**: ≤1.50 mm needle-tip error, as the injection port radius is 1.50 mm (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023).
- **Vial grasping and placement**: The KUKA system achieved 0.12 mm calibrated accuracy sufficient for 100% success on 10 mL GC vials (pqac-00000012).
- **Solid dispensing (mass tolerance rather than position)**: ±2 mg at 20 mg targets; 0.07% mean error at 200 mg for non-challenging solids (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031).
- **Mobile base coarse positioning**: ±10 mm and ±2.5° before fine arm calibration (pqac-00000027).

**Explicit gap**: No study reports the positioning tolerance required for swapping vial carriers on a pipetting gantry, loading well plates into plate readers, or changing augers/hoppers on a powder doser as a reproducible benchmark with a defined tolerance threshold. These tasks appear in descriptions of SDL workflows but without quantified manipulation requirements.

## 3. Station Recalibration Methods

Three distinct approaches to recalibration at each station have been published:

**Touch-sensitive calibration cubes (Burger et al., 2020)**: The KUKA LBR iiwa touches six points on three mutually perpendicular faces of a calibration cube at each station, and the recorded contact points define the station coordinate frame relative to the robot. With initial position noise of up to ±15 mm and orientation noise of ±2.5°, the cube was located to within 0.12 mm and orientation offsets were reduced below 0.005° (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000038). This is the closest published analog to an AprilTag-based calibration square, but uses force feedback rather than vision.

**AprilTag coarse localization plus visual servoing (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; DOI: 10.1109/IROS55552.2023.10341743)**: An AprilTag brought the end effector near the injection target, then two fixed cameras and a Keypoint-RCNN model detected the syringe needle and iteratively servoed to submillimeter alignment. This achieved 100% injection success over 63 trials, while the AprilTag-only approach achieved only 9.52% (2160p) and 4.76% (1080p) (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023). This demonstrates that AprilTag-only localization is insufficient for millimeter-precision tasks and must be supplemented with closed-loop visual refinement.

**Semantic object models with precision fixtures (OSCAR, Pivin et al., 2026)**: Each piece of labware is characterized in a Semantic Object Description Format (SODF) encoding 3D shape, interaction points, and forces. Objects are anchored with precision shoulder screws and 3D-printed supports; the system then uses position and force control to interact with them (pqac-00000054). This is a teaching-agnostic approach where new layouts require re-fixturing rather than re-programming.

**ALVAR fiducial tags (Joshi, 2021)**: ALVAR tags attached to objects supported object detection and pose estimation in a dual-arm system using cameras, Kinect, and force/torque sensors (pqac-00000010). This is the most direct precedent for AprilTag-based fiducial-guided motion in a laboratory manipulator context.

**Explicit gap**: No publication describes a system that uses AprilTags (specifically) as calibration squares at each station in a materials-science SDL to recalibrate a low-cost arm before each task, as the user describes. The Angelopoulos approach is the closest, but uses AprilTags only for coarse approach, not as the primary calibration target.

Reported demonstration budgets and success rates are kept distinct from qualitative demonstrations and chemical-yield outcomes.*

### 4.1 Teach Pendant and Scripted Waypoints

The dominant approach in published SDL work is deterministic programming via teach pendants or scripted waypoints. Burger et al. used station-specific programs with six-point tactile recalibration (pqac-00000038). Joshi (2021) described the ABB YuMi's RS-2 system where "job teaching" stores motion elements, labware-specific gripper indices, and reference points, explicitly rejecting path planning as "unsafe, difficult to reconfigure, computationally demanding" (pqac-00000008). OSCAR's approach generates robot behaviors from digital models of labware and a calibrated workspace map rather than from device-specific waypoint recording (pqac-00000054). This yields extremely high reliability where tested (464/464, 400/400), but the programming time per new task is not measured in any study.

### 4.2 Imitation Learning Policies on Low-Cost Arms

The most directly relevant study for the user's setup is Cowling (2026; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170; **preprint**), which evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0.5 on an SO-101 leader/follower arm (approximately $200 in parts) using LeRobot's implementations. The task was picking up a green ball while ignoring two red distractors and placing it in a basket, with success defined as delivery within 30 seconds. One operator recorded 225 demonstrations by leader-follower teleoperation at 30 fps; each demonstration lasted approximately 17 seconds. Nested training sets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations were evaluated on 10 fixed placements (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000053).

Key results (pqac-00000056):
- **ACT from scratch**: 1/40 (2.5%) at 12 demos → 37/40 (92.5%) at 100 demos, with an odds ratio of 3.89 per doubling of data. This is the recommended LeRobot baseline for ≥100 demonstrations.
- **π0.5 expert-only fine-tuning**: 16/40 (40%) at 12 demos → 28/40 (70%) at 25 demos, then stable around 68–75%. This provides a large advantage with scarce data but saturates below ACT's peak.
- **Diffusion Policy (trimmed)**: Peaked at 25/50 (50%) with 50 demonstrations but was non-monotonic. Untrimmed data yielded only 3/110 successes; removing a median 2.8 s idle lead-in was essential.
- **SmolVLA**: Peaked at 21/40 (52.5%) at 50 demos and declined with more data.
- **π0.5 LoRA fine-tuning**: 4/110 total successes; this recipe largely failed.

The study's evaluation protocol is reproducible: each block comprised one checkpoint run once on each of 10 placements in order, with a 30-second limit per episode and a 20-second reset. All 1,340 main-comparison episodes were scored and audited against recordings (pqac-00000053).

**Explicit gap**: No published work has applied ACT, Diffusion Policy, or any LeRobot-style imitation-learning policy to a laboratory instrument task (e.g., capping, pipetting, weighing, plate loading) on a low-cost arm. The Cowling study used a pick-and-place task with distractor objects, not a chemistry workflow. Extending these results to the constrained, precision-demanding tasks of an SDL requires new experiments.

### 4.3 Reinforcement Learning

Pizzuto et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1109/CASE59546.2024.10711291) demonstrated model-free RL (TQC with Hindsight Experience Replay) for vial scraping on a Franka Emika Panda. The policy used proprioceptive feedback and force/torque readings; no human demonstrations were required. The real-robot case study succeeded with two vial sizes and two scraper lengths, with each full-vial scrape taking approximately 90 minutes across 24 regions (pqac-00000051). Curriculum learning was essential for generalizing across starting poses (pqac-00000049). No repeated-trial success percentage was reported; the only non-recoverable failure was a stuck scraper requiring human reset (pqac-00000052).

Lei et al. (2026; DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.aed6267) achieved 1000/1000 successful episodes across eight manipulation tasks by combining diffusion-policy imitation learning with offline and online RL. Per task, approximately 115 demonstrations (1.8 hours of human teleoperation), 566 offline RL rollouts (6.5 hours), and 434 online RL rollouts (5.6 hours) were needed—approximately 13.9 hours total (pqac-00000004). This was not demonstrated in an SDL context, but the protocol establishes a reproducible benchmark for deployment-grade manipulation learning.

## 5. Cost Considerations

**No published cost-per-task metric exists** for comparing robot arms in SDL applications. The literature provides only broad cost ranges:

- Commercial articulated robots (KUKA, ABB, UR, Franka) are described as generally costing approximately $20,000–$40,000 for the arm alone (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000044). Complete mobile platforms such as the KUKA KMR are substantially more expensive (generally considered over $100,000).
- Burger's thesis notes that combining a MiR mobile base with a UR5 or Franka Panda provides "a dexterous collaborative mobile robot similar to the KMR at a lower purchase price" but gives no figures (pqac-00000040).
- 3D-printed and open-source robotic arms range from $50 (DeltaZ) to $700 (anthropomorphic arm with vision-based manipulation) (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).
- The SO-101 arm used in the Cowling (2026) study costs "a few hundred dollars in parts" (pqac-00000009).

**Explicit gap**: No study compares the cost per task—or cost per successfully completed laboratory operation—between industry-standard arms (UR5e at ~$35k, Franka Panda at ~$30k, ABB YuMi at ~$40k) and low-cost alternatives (AgileX PiPER at ~$2k, SO-101 at ~$200). Such a metric would need to account for arm cost, integration time, programming or training time per task, success rate, cycle time, and maintenance. This represents a significant gap that the user's work could fill.

## 6. Reproducible Test Protocols Identified

Based on the literature, the following tests can be reproduced by anyone validating an affordable arm for SDL use:

1. **Vial grasp-and-place (Burger protocol)**: Grasp 10 mL GC vials from a rack, navigate to a target station, and place into a receiving rack. Repeat for N iterations. Measure: success/failure (vial placed without dropping); number of trials ≥400; success criterion: vial seated in well; measuring tool: visual inspection or force-feedback contact confirmation (pqac-00000011).

2. **Cartridge/hopper insertion (Burger protocol)**: Place a cartridge into a cavity with 0.5 mm clearance. Measure: successful insertion (cartridge seated); number of trials ≥400; success criterion: cartridge detected in position; measuring tool: force-feedback confirmation (pqac-00000011).

3. **Syringe injection alignment (Angelopoulos protocol)**: Align a syringe needle with a 1.50 mm radius target. Measure: XY planar distance between needle tip and target center after alignment; number of trials ≥63; success criterion: needle tip within 1.50 mm of target center; measuring tool: two calibrated machine-vision cameras with Keypoint-RCNN detection (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024).

4. **Solid dispensing accuracy (Jiang protocol)**: Dispense 13 different solids at multiple target weights (1000, 500, 200, 20 mg). Measure: percentage dispensing error = (dispensed − target)/target × 100; number of runs: 120 total; success criterion: completed procedure within mass tolerance; measuring tool: analytical balance; failure criterion: non-completion of one procedure (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000033).

5. **Imitation-learning data-efficiency scaling (Cowling protocol)**: Train ACT/Diffusion Policy/foundation models on nested demonstration sets of 12, 25, 50, 100, 200 episodes. Evaluate each checkpoint on 10 fixed placements with a 30-second time limit. Measure: successes/episodes with 95% Wilson score intervals; criterion: target object delivered to goal; measuring tool: operator scoring audited against camera recordings (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000056).

6. **Six-point calibration accuracy (Burger protocol)**: Touch six points on three perpendicular faces of a calibration cube with known initial noise. Measure: residual position error (mm) and orientation error (degrees); measuring tool: force-feedback contact detection; success criterion: frame located within specification (pqac-00000012).

## 7. Explicit Gaps in the Published Literature

The following specific gaps were identified where **no published evidence exists**:

1. **No study has used imitation learning (ACT, Diffusion Policy, or any LeRobot policy) for a laboratory instrument task** such as capping, pipetting, weighing, or plate loading on any arm, let alone a low-cost one.

2. **No cost-per-task metric** has been published comparing industry-standard and affordable arms for SDL operations.

3. **No study has used AprilTags as the primary calibration target** (calibration square) at each station for a robot arm in a materials-science SDL. The Angelopoulos AprilTag + visual-servoing approach and Burger's touch-calibration-cube approach are the closest analogs.

4. **No study has benchmarked an AgileX PiPER or SO-101 arm** on any laboratory instrument task. The SO-101 has been evaluated only on a pick-and-place task with distractor objects.

5. **No study reports positioning tolerance requirements for swapping vial carriers on a pipetting gantry**, loading/unloading augers or hoppers on a powder doser, or performing tool changes in a materials-science context as reproducible benchmarks.

6. **Task-level success rates are rarely reported** with sufficient statistical rigor: Burger (100%, ≥400 trials), Angelopoulos (100%, 63 trials), and Jiang (76.9%, 120 runs) are exceptions. Most SDL papers describe workflow demonstrations without systematic success/failure counting.

7. **Setup time and programming time per new task** are not measured in any SDL robotics paper. This information is essential for comparing the value proposition of teach-pendant programming against imitation learning but is entirely absent from the literature.

snippets: The workflow requires a manipulator that is capable of transporting and manipulating both vials and racks.
It is further required to handle powder cartridges and to load powder cartridges into the solid dispensing system
The challenge is to find a commercially available robotic system that can both reach individual modules and perform complex manipulations robustly.

When this project was started in 2016, there was a single commercial collaborative mobile manipulator available, that was deemed capable of navigating and manipulation robustly using commercially available software packages, the KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR) [12].

Alternative mobile robots to the KMR have been commercialized during this work. For example, there is the MIR robot [15]. These, combined with a collaborative arm such as the UR5 or Panda, make for a dexterous collaborative mobile robot similar to the KMR at a lower purchase price.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes adding and adapting tasks through diffusion-based imitation learning from human demonstrations, followed by offline and online real-world reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. It does not describe teach-pendant programming, scripted waypoint authoring, AprilTag/fiducial-guided motion, or specific ACT policies. The demonstrated approach begins with a human-grounded diffusion policy rather than learning from scratch, using demonstrations to constrain exploration to physically plausible actions. Across eight real-world manipulation tasks, the authors report an average of approximately 115 human demonstrations per task, requiring about 1.8 hours of human data collection. This is followed by approximately 566 offline-RL rollouts (6.5 hours) and 434 online-RL rollouts (5.6 hours) per task. Thus, the reported total per-task effort is roughly 13.9 hours, with most data generated autonomously rather than by teleoperators. Across all tasks, human collection accounted for 804 episodes and 12.5 hours, or about 13% of a total data-collection budget under 100 hours. The excerpt presents these figures as sufficient for deployment-grade performance, but it does not provide a generic task-onboarding procedure, exact setup/calibration time, or a direct comparison against waypoint-, fiducial-, or teach-pendant-based methods.

contexts.context: The excerpt addresses imitation-learning policies for adding a task to a low-cost laboratory robot arm, specifically ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0.5. It does not compare these approaches with teach pendants, scripted waypoints, or fiducial-guided motion using AprilTags, and it provides no measurements of setup time, programming time, or demonstration-recording time. In the reported experiment, the researchers teleoperated 225 demonstrations of one pick-and-place task with distractor objects, then evaluated nested training sets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations. Data requirements varied substantially by policy and training recipe: ACT trained from scratch improved from 1/40 successes at 12 demonstrations to 37/40 at 100, while fine-tuned π0.5 performed best with scarce data, achieving 16/40 at 12 and 28/40 at 25, then remaining near 70%. SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaked around 50%, with startup failures affecting both. The study emphasizes that results are task- and setup-specific, compare fixed recipes rather than ideal architectures, and are confounded by fixed training length: larger datasets were seen fewer times. Thus, the excerpt supports a demonstration range of 12–200 for imitation-learning experiments, but cannot establish a universal number of demonstrations or the practical setup time for any task.

contexts.context: The excerpt evaluates imitation-learning policies for adding a task to a low-cost laboratory robot arm, specifically ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and pretrained π0.5. It does not discuss teach pendants, scripted waypoints, AprilTags, fiducial-guided motion, or the operator/setup time required by those approaches. Demonstration budgets range from 12 to 200 demonstrations. The clearest practical guidance is that pretrained fine-tuning is advantageous below roughly 50 demonstrations, while ACT trained from scratch generally needs between 50 and 100 demonstrations to learn this task. At 100 or more demonstrations, ACT is recommended as a baseline, though comparisons depend strongly on training recipe and exposure. Diffusion Policy was evaluated across the same budgets, but its results were confounded because the number of training passes changed with dataset size; trimming idle lead-in frames substantially improved its ability to initiate motion, from 4% to 90% of episodes. The paper emphasizes that more data alone cannot be cleanly separated from reduced training exposure, and that the required amount may depend on the policy, fine-tuning method, and task. No quantitative setup-duration or demonstration-collection-time estimate is provided.

For more advanced dexterous tasks, such as Adapt Hand pick-and-place, demonstrations are collected through human teleoperation using an Apple Vision Pro headset and hand/wrist tracking, with signals mapped into the simulator. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that new laboratory-robot tasks are added primarily through job teaching with the robot’s teach pendant, rather than through imitation-learning policies, AprilTag/fiducial-guided motion, or a fully scripted waypoint/path-planning system. Direct manipulation was explicitly rejected, and path-planning approaches were considered unsafe, difficult to reconfigure, computationally demanding, and dependent on detailed environment and robot models. To reduce programming effort, the RS-2 design teaches a common transfer path once and stores multiple motion elements together. Labware-specific gripper positions are selected through variable indices, while destinations are handled by mapping a basic taught motion to ALP reference points. New labware can therefore be incorporated by adding a variable index, and new ALP destinations by adding a reference point, without changing earlier programming. Each arm has separate reference points because the arms use different end effectors and postures. The excerpt does not report a fixed number of demonstrations: the method is teach-pendant programming rather than demonstration-based learning. It also does not provide a numerical setup time. Qualitatively, the comparison rates development time for the selected job-teaching approach as moderate, while teaching effort is moderate; path planning and offline planning receive different tradeoffs. Motion files are transferred automatically before a process and deleted afterward.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the platform as the Fetch Mobile Manipulator Robot, whose configuration includes a differential-drive base and a 7-DoF arm mounted on a liftable torso. The system uses two Toshiba TeliCam machine-vision cameras. For positioning, the robot first navigates to the chemistry equipment and uses an AprilTag to bring the end effector near the injection port. The task also required the syringe height to be some ε above the target before lowering and orientational alignment in which the syringe and target Z axes are anti-parallel. contexts.context: The excerpt reports that the proposed mobile-manipulation method aligned a syringe needle with a target such as a gas-chromatography injection port with submillimeter positioning accuracy. It achieved a 100% injection success rate and was, on average, more than 11 times as accurate as simpler methods that relied only on an AprilTag and a calibrated target pose. The calibration and positioning approach combined an AprilTag for initial end-effector positioning with needle detection from two machine-vision cameras, followed by image-based visual servoing that moved the end effector until the needle was aligned with the target. The excerpt also states that the approach was robust to syringe grasping errors and mobile-base navigation errors. It does not specify the exact numerical positioning error, the robot-arm model, or a separate injection error-tolerance threshold. The only tolerance-like accuracy figure provided here is the qualitative submillimeter alignment claim. The needle detector itself had validation L1 losses of 0.75 pixels for the base keypoint and 1.64 pixels for the tip keypoint, corresponding to at most 0.15% and 0.32% of the image width, respectively; these are image-detection errors rather than the overall injection positioning tolerance.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a multi-robot laboratory setup involving a mobile KUKA arm and an ABB IRB 14000 YuMi dual-arm robot. The KUKA system has seven degrees of freedom, a 14 kg payload, and a custom gripper designed to grasp glass vials from the top or side and lock into racks. Its mobile base navigates between stations using laser-scanned maps, saved locations, nodes, edges, and waypoints. The system includes collision detection and emergency stopping for both the arm and base. Reported mobile-robot positioning precision was ±10 mm, with orientation precision below ±2.5°. More precise arm calibration was achieved using calibration cubes and six-point force-feedback calibration. The ABB YuMi is a stationary, seven-axis dual-arm robot fitted with ABB SmartGrippers; neoprene adhesive was added to the flat fingers to reduce slippage. It was mounted over an optical breadboard so racks and objects could be positioned in a fixed workspace. contexts.context: This excerpt describes the dual-arm robot’s solid-dispensing workflow but does not report the positioning tolerance or the overall success rate for the ABB YuMi system. The system tasks included opening and closing the analytical-balance door, moving an empty receiving vial onto the balance, transporting the material hopper to the dispensing position, mixing the powder to break up agglomerates, selecting a spatula based on the remaining target mass, scooping powder, and dispensing it through a funnel into the vial. Excess powder was returned to the hopper, while substantial over-dispensing triggered a reset in which the vial’s contents were returned. Accuracy was controlled using closed-loop weighing: the pre-dispensing weight was recorded, the difference between target and current weight (ΔW/DW) determined the dispensing behavior and spatula choice, and a fuzzy controller adjusted spatula tilting and shaking using this error and particle-size information. Dispensing stopped when the measured weight error was within the specified acceptable tolerance. The excerpt identifies the analytical balance as the measurement instrument, but it does not provide numerical accuracy results, positioning tolerances, or success-rate statistics.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Jiang et al.’s dual-arm robotic platform as an autonomous solid-dispensing system benchmarked against Quantos and Chemspeed. It dispensed thirteen different solids at multiple target weights, including sodium nitrite tests at 1000, 500, 200, and 20 mg with a 2 mg tolerance. The system used robotic manipulation of vials, hoppers, scales, doors, funnels, and differently sized spatulas; dispensing could be restarted when over-dispensing occurred. Accuracy was evaluated using average percentage dispensing error, with standard deviation, calculated from the target and dispensed weights (the excerpt refers to eqn (2)). Weighing performance was therefore assessed through the balance reading and the resulting mass error. A dispensing failure was defined as non-completion of one procedure, and failures were counted over runs for the thirteen materials; causes included blocked funnels or spatula outlets, deliquescent material sticking to surfaces, and robot errors when the balance showed no change during continuous dispensing. The excerpt does not state the system’s positioning tolerance or provide the numerical overall success rate, although it indicates that failure counts were summarized over 120 runs. It reports 0.07% average error for non-challenging solids at a 200 mg target.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the evaluation of Jiang et al.’s biomimetic dual-arm dispensing platform against Quantos and Chemspeed systems, using thirteen solids and multiple target dispensing weights. It does not state the ABB YuMi system’s positioning tolerance or an overall success rate, nor does it specify the robot’s individual manipulation tasks in sufficient detail. The reported dispensing-accuracy measure was percentage weighing error, calculated as (dispensed mass − target mass) divided by target mass, multiplied by 100. Positive values indicated over-dispensing and negative values indicated under-dispensing. Failures, including cases where no material was dispensed, were included in the average results and could produce a 100% error; Figure 6 represented total non-dispensing as −100%. A dispensing procedure that was not completed was classified as a failure, and solids with failure rates above 10% were classified as challenging for that platform. The system was assessed across inorganic and organic materials, including abrasive and moisture-sensitive powders. At a 200 mg target, the biomimetic robot performed better on average than the commercial benchmark systems for non-challenging solids, while performance became approximately comparable when challenging solids were included.

In this workflow, the YuMi robot transported sample vials from a rack to a Grinding Station, handled grinding, unscrewed the vial caps, and placed the caps into a plate in the Sample Preparation Station. Solid-dispensing performance was assessed gravimetrically: Kapton-taped caps were weighed before processing, the samples were shaken with the caps facing downward, and the caps were reweighed after 2, 4, 8, and 16 minutes. The mass difference represented the amount of solid transferred to each cap. The study found little average difference between 2 and 16 minutes of shaking and reported approximately 10% transfer after 2 minutes. Assuming 10 mg is needed for suitable organic-sample PXRD data, it estimated that roughly 100 mg of starting material would be required. The described feasibility study concerns manipulation of 10 mL Agilent GC vials and custom racks. The gripper must grasp vials from above and sideways, including in tight spaces, and grasp racks top-down using an electronic parallel gripper. The excerpt does not specify the number of stations, the number of experiments, or an overall task success rate for the Burger 2020 Nature paper, so those details cannot be established from this passage. Recalibration is performed using KUKA’s six-point (6P) touch-sensitive method: the robot touches a calibration cube at six locations across three mutually perpendicular planes, records the contact points, and solves the resulting equations to define the cube’s coordinate frame relative to the robot. Testing with noisy initial position estimates found the cube within 0.12 mm and corrected orientation offsets to below 0.005 degrees. The passage also notes that cartridge manipulation was not included in this initial study.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies two principal robot-arm architectures used in self-driving laboratories: six-axis articulated arms, also called six-degrees-of-freedom (DOF) arms, and SCARAs (Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arms). SCARAs use a central column and two rotational joints for XY-plane movement, vertical Z-axis actuation, and a compliant end-effector joint. They are characterized as rapid and high-precision, making them suitable for speed- and repeatability-dependent tasks that do not require complex spatial manipulation. Six-DOF articulated arms provide mostly unconstrained positioning and greater flexibility, but at the expense of speed and kinematic simplicity. The article states that their versatility allows them to connect SDL instruments and perform tasks such as vial transfers, reagent addition, and operation of otherwise manual instruments. However, the supplied pages do not provide specific commercial or manufacturer model names, purchase or operating costs, numerical positioning-accuracy or repeatability specifications, or a model-by-model comparison. Thus, these pages support only a qualitative comparison: SCARAs are associated with rapid, high-precision, repeatable motion, while six-DOF arms are associated with flexible positioning and sophisticated manipulation.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that Pizzuto et al. used model-free reinforcement learning for the laboratory task of scraping crystallized powder from vial walls. The approach was first developed in a scenario-specific simulation using a Franka Emika Panda robot and a laboratory scraper inserted into a simulated vial, followed by training and evaluation on a real robotic manipulator across different laboratory setups. The learned policy mapped proprioceptive and force observations to end-effector displacement actions, addressing the need for fine-grained motion and force-sensitive adaptation during scraping. The authors also investigated curriculum learning, progressively expanding the workspace as performance improved in order to reduce training costs and increase task success. However, the provided pages do not specify the numerical success rates, the number of demonstrations, the detailed experimental protocol, the total number of trials, or the precise success criterion used for the reported Franka Panda experiments. Those details would need to be obtained from later sections of the paper, likely the experimental setup and results.
contexts.question: What success rates and number of demonstrations are reported for Pizzuto 2024 reinforcement learning for sample scraping on a Franka Panda? What was the protocol, number of trials, and success criterion?

contexts.context: The excerpt reports a contact-rich vial-scraping benchmark using a 7-DOF Franka Emika Panda with an attached scraper. The simulated task requires translating along the vial’s z-axis while maintaining wall contact (“Fy ≥ Cthreshold”); trajectories last 50 timesteps, with randomized goals and resets. Success is evaluated every 1,000 test episodes across five random seeds, reporting mean success rate, return, and standard error for TQC and SAC with HER. Rewards are \(R_{\text{sim}}=R_{\text{goal}}+w_0R_{\text{contact}}+w_1R_{\text{vial}}\); vial movement ≥2 cm incurs penalty. No positioning tolerance, demonstrations, setup time, or cost-per-task is reported.
contexts.question:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

New tasks at each station: What published work has one arm take over several hands-on laboratory tasks at different instruments (swapping vial carriers on a pipetting gantry, augers or hoppers on a powder doser, tool changers, capping, weighing, loading plates), what positioning tolerance did each task need, and what success rates were reported? How were new tasks added (teach pendant or scripted waypoints, fiducial-guided motion, or imitation-learning policies such as ACT, diffusion policy or LeRobot policies), how many demonstrations or how much setup time did each need, and how do they compare on the same task?

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. contexts.context: This excerpt describes a reproducible LeRobot vision-policy benchmark, not laboratory manipulation. Policies used two 224×224 camera images, 30-Hz control, 50-action chunks, and ten flow-matching inference steps. Testing comprised 1,070 episodes/97 blocks from 86 models; each episode had ten placements, a 30-s limit, and 20-s reset. Success meant “Green ball delivered to the basket within 30 seconds.” Across 1,340 episodes, 463 succeeded, with 282 initiation, 259 location, 161 grip, and 127 collision failures. Automatic wrist-camera measures distinguished reaching and carrying; operator labels conflicted with recordings in 2.0% of episodes. No arm-model or laboratory-task tolerance/cost evidence is provided.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports model-free deep reinforcement learning for autonomous robotic scraping of powder from sample vials. A simulated environment was transferred to a real manipulator; the policy worked across different vial sizes and scraper tools. The scraper’s small contact area and restricted, slower motion reduced glass-breakage risk. One unrecoverable failure occurred when the scraper stuck and lacked force to withdraw, requiring human reset. Figures show initial, partial, and fully scraped vials, but this excerpt gives no arm model, trial count, success percentage, positioning tolerance, demonstrations, setup time, cost, or DOI. Future work includes visual rewards, alternative tools, and bimanual vial rotation/scraping.

contexts.context: OSCAR (ACS Synthetic Biology 2026, DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733) demonstrates one UR3 performing three molecular-biology protocols across a thermocycler, pipette stations, gel electrophoresis, touchscreen, Petri dish, and colony picking. contexts.question:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

New tasks at each station: What published work has one arm take over several hands-on laboratory tasks at different instruments (swapping vial carriers on a pipetting gantry, augers or hoppers on a powder doser, tool changers, capping, weighing, loading plates), what positioning tolerance did each task need, and what success rates were reported? How were new tasks added (teach pendant or scripted waypoints, fiducial-guided motion, or imitation-learning policies such as ACT, diffusion policy or LeRobot policies), how many demonstrations or how much setup time did each need, and how do they compare on the same task?

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports a repeatable manipulation benchmark: episodes tested whether the arm moved, grasped a ball, carried it, and delivered it; scores were audited across 1,340 episodes, correcting 27 (2.0%), reducing successes from 473 to 463. Success rates used Wilson 95% intervals, Fisher/Newcombe comparisons, logistic regression versus log2 demonstrations, and exact McNemar tests. With 40 episodes/cell, resolution was roughly ±15 percentage points. ACT improved from 1/40 successes at 12 demonstrations to 37/40 at 100; π0.5 expert-only reached 28/40 at 25. SmolVLA peaked at 21/40; trimmed Diffusion Policy at 25/50.

# Tests and Benchmarks for Robot Arms as Automated Manual Manipulators in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Robot Arms Performing Multiple Hands-On Tasks at Different Stations

The most comprehensive demonstration of a single arm taking over several hands-on laboratory tasks at different instruments is the mobile robotic chemist by Burger et al. (2020), which used a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on a KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR) platform. Over eight days it autonomously performed 688 experiments across multiple stations encompassing weighing and dispensing insoluble solids, dispensing liquid solutions, transporting sample vials in racks, capping vials under nitrogen, sonication for catalyst dispersion, photolysis, and transferring samples to a head-space gas chromatograph (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). In robustness tests the system achieved 464/464 successful vial grasps and placements and 400/400 successful cartridge grasps and placements at both the hotel and the Quantos dispenser, over 29 and 25 iterations respectively (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 69-73). The cartridge cavity was only 0.5 mm larger than the cartridge, implying a placement tolerance of approximately 0.25 mm (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 69-73). The arm had a stated repeatability of 0.1 mm, and after six-point touch-sensitive calibration against a reference cube, the station frame was located to within 0.12 mm with orientation residuals below 0.005° (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56).

Jiang et al. (2023; DOI: 10.1039/D3DD00075C) demonstrated an ABB YuMi dual-arm robot performing biomimetic solid dispensing. Tasks included opening and closing an analytical-balance door, moving vials and hoppers, selecting and manipulating spatulas of different sizes, scooping powder, dispensing through a funnel, and closed-loop weighing (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 3-4). The system dispensed thirteen different solids at target weights down to 20 ± 2 mg. For non-challenging solids at 200 mg, the mean dispensing error was 0.07%; across all solids the mean failure rate was 23.1% over 120 runs, where failure was defined as non-completion of one dispensing procedure (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11). Failure causes included blocked funnels, deliquescent material, and robot errors when the balance showed no weight change during continuous dispensing (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10).

Lunt et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1039/D3SC06206F) presented a multi-robot integration for a 12-step PXRD workflow using an ABB YuMi and KUKA KMR. The YuMi transferred vials from transport racks to a grinding station, carried out grinding-related handling, unscrewed vial caps, and placed caps into a plate at the sample-preparation station (lunt2024aroboticworkflow pages 87-95). The KMR provided mobile base precision of ±10 mm and orientation below ±2.5°, with fine calibration achieved via force-feedback six-point calibration cubes (lunt2024aroboticworkflow pages 49-57). No task-level success rate was reported for this system.

ORGANA (Darvish et al., 2025; DOI: 10.1016/j.matt.2024.10.015) used a Franka robot to perform solubility screening (7 steps, 25.63 min), recrystallization (8 steps, 44.80 min), pH measurement (6 steps, 3.85 min), and electrochemistry including electrode polishing (114 steps, 130 min) (darvish2025organaarobotic pages 14-15). No positioning tolerance or success rate was reported.

OSCAR (Pivin et al., 2026; DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733) used a UR3 arm to perform pipetting (1–200 µL), tip handling, PCR thermocycler programming via a stylus tool, gel electrophoresis loading, Petri-dish manipulation, spreading, and colony picking across three multistep biology protocols. The same protocols were successfully replanned for UR5 and Franka Panda arms, with average planning time of approximately 5 s across all three arm models (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 7-8). No positioning tolerance or task-level success rate was reported.

Lim et al. (2021; DOI: 10.1109/TASE.2020.3036055) used a Denso VS-060 6-DOF arm to automate a Michael reaction, performing syringe-pump liquid transfer, mixing on a magnetic stirrer, silica/cotton filtration, and vial transfer to a GC-MS autoinjector rack. The robot achieved a yield of 34%, which was stated to be "comparable to that obtained by a junior chemist (undergraduate student in Chemistry)" (lim2021developmentofa pages 1-2). No positioning tolerance was reported; yields rather than manipulation success rates served as the outcome metric.

## 2. Positioning Tolerances by Task

The literature reveals a hierarchy of positioning demands:

- **Cartridge/hopper placement into powder dispensers**: ~0.25 mm, as the cavity clearance is only 0.5 mm larger than the cartridge (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 69-73).
- **Syringe injection into a GC port**: ≤1.50 mm needle-tip error, as the injection port radius is 1.50 mm (angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 2-3, angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 4-6).
- **Vial grasping and placement**: The KUKA system achieved 0.12 mm calibrated accuracy sufficient for 100% success on 10 mL GC vials (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56).
- **Solid dispensing (mass tolerance rather than position)**: ±2 mg at 20 mg targets; 0.07% mean error at 200 mg for non-challenging solids (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 8-10, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 2-3).
- **Mobile base coarse positioning**: ±10 mm and ±2.5° before fine arm calibration (lunt2024aroboticworkflow pages 49-57).

**Explicit gap**: No study reports the positioning tolerance required for swapping vial carriers on a pipetting gantry, loading well plates into plate readers, or changing augers/hoppers on a powder doser as a reproducible benchmark with a defined tolerance threshold. These tasks appear in descriptions of SDL workflows but without quantified manipulation requirements.

## 3. Station Recalibration Methods

Three distinct approaches to recalibration at each station have been published:

**Touch-sensitive calibration cubes (Burger et al., 2020)**: The KUKA LBR iiwa touches six points on three mutually perpendicular faces of a calibration cube at each station, and the recorded contact points define the station coordinate frame relative to the robot. With initial position noise of up to ±15 mm and orientation noise of ±2.5°, the cube was located to within 0.12 mm and orientation offsets were reduced below 0.005° (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). This is the closest published analog to an AprilTag-based calibration square, but uses force feedback rather than vision.

**AprilTag coarse localization plus visual servoing (Angelopoulos et al., 2023; DOI: 10.1109/IROS55552.2023.10341743)**: An AprilTag brought the end effector near the injection target, then two fixed cameras and a Keypoint-RCNN model detected the syringe needle and iteratively servoed to submillimeter alignment. This achieved 100% injection success over 63 trials, while the AprilTag-only approach achieved only 9.52% (2160p) and 4.76% (1080p) (angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 7-8, angelopoulos2023highaccuracyinjectionusing pages 4-6). This demonstrates that AprilTag-only localization is insufficient for millimeter-precision tasks and must be supplemented with closed-loop visual refinement.

**Semantic object models with precision fixtures (OSCAR, Pivin et al., 2026)**: Each piece of labware is characterized in a Semantic Object Description Format (SODF) encoding 3D shape, interaction points, and forces. Objects are anchored with precision shoulder screws and 3D-printed supports; the system then uses position and force control to interact with them (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 3-5). This is a teaching-agnostic approach where new layouts require re-fixturing rather than re-programming.

**ALVAR fiducial tags (Joshi, 2021)**: ALVAR tags attached to objects supported object detection and pose estimation in a dual-arm system using cameras, Kinect, and force/torque sensors (joshi2021optimizationandapplication pages 35-39). This is the most direct precedent for AprilTag-based fiducial-guided motion in a laboratory manipulator context.

**Explicit gap**: No publication describes a system that uses AprilTags (specifically) as calibration squares at each station in a materials-science SDL to recalibrate a low-cost arm before each task, as the user describes. The Angelopoulos approach is the closest, but uses AprilTags only for coarse approach, not as the primary calibration target.
